Article Title: Palantir CEO Alex Karp says AI may be creating ‘America's biggest problem’ by making …
Article Text:
Alex Karp: AI is creating a 'complete decoupling' of wealth

Palantir CEO Alex Karp recently warned that AI is creating a widening wealth gap, with the biggest gains going to those developing the technology. Speaking in an interview with Axel Springer CEO Mathias Döpfner, Karp said this growing inequality is the "biggest problem" in the United States and added that AI is being oversold, as not everyone will benefit equally from the technology despite its potential to improve lives. "While it will raise the standard of living of the average person, the people involved are likely to get 10, 100 times wealthier than they already are," Alex Karp said. He further stated that this AI wealth disparity is the "biggest problem in this country."Alex Karp also criticised how AI is being promoted. “The overselling of AI in this country is really, really, really, somewhat disconcerting, but it's also depressing because you don't have to do it,” he said, describing AI as a “natural resource” with both positive and negative potential.During the interview, Alex Karp said earlier technological revolutions also created wealth, but the gap between the richest people and everyone else was much smaller. “The person at the bottom, maybe their salary doubled, and the person at the top became five times wealthier, but it was very unusual to be a billionaire 40 years ago,” Karp said.He further added: “You now have a revolution where, you know, I could become 20 times wealthier than I am now.”Alex Karp said AI is creating a “complete decoupling” between ordinary economic gains and a small group of people who achieve "unimaginable wealth." He also said many people worry about AI because some of the industry's leading figures have warned that the technology could disrupt jobs.“The people running the lab companies, who are the leaders, told you it's true,” Alex Karp said. “They're telling you your life is going to suck. And they're also getting very wealthy, and you don't find them very likable.”While Karp did not name anyone, executives including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman have previously warned that AI could disrupt jobs, though both have recently softened their comments.He also took a swipe at some of the people leading the AI industry. “These are like very oddly-shaped-IQ specimens that you probably wouldn't want to have over for dinner,” Karp said. “And if they were over for the dinner, you have nothing to talk to them about. And, by the way, vice versa.”
Article Summary: Palantir CEO Alex Karp said AI is creating a 'complete decoupling' of wealth. He said the biggest gains are going to those developing the technology. Karp also criticised how AI is being promoted in the U.S.

Article Title: OnePlus may shut down in US, Europe within days; parent company Oppo to take over
Article Text:
OnePlus is reportedly exiting the US and Europe, with India left as the brand's biggest surviving market.

What happens to your OnePlus phone if the brand exits

The signs OnePlus was winding down have been piling up all year

OnePlus, the brand that once sold flagship specs at half the price and dared everyone else to keep up, is reportedly about to stop selling phones in the US and Europe altogether. German outlet WinFuture, citing well-informed sources, reports that OnePlus and parent company Oppo will announce "fundamental changes" to their strategy in the coming days—corporate language that, in practice, means a full withdrawal from two of the brand's most visible markets.Closed-door press briefings have already happened, according to the report, though company representatives apparently declined to explain why the brand is being pulled. India and China were left conspicuously unaddressed too. The expectation is that OnePlus continues in both as a product line inside Oppo—cheaper phones, tablets, no independent identity. India is the reason it survives at all. The country accounts for well over half of OnePlus's annual sales, and the Nord series still sells hard in the mid-range.Existing owners aren't being cut loose immediately. OnePlus and Oppo told the press that software updates and after-sales support will continue for already-sold devices until the end of their respective lifecycles. What ends is everything ahead of that—no new launches, no fresh stock, no local marketing. Remaining inventory in Europe and the US is being sold off over the coming weeks and months, and OnePlus's European online stores are already close to empty.None of this arrives out of nowhere. Android Headlines reported in January that OnePlus was being dismantled; the company denied it. 9to5Google reported in March that operations could cease in global markets as early as April. India CEO Robin Liu left the same month. By April, OnePlus admitted it was "evaluating its regional roadmap and product strategy" in Europe. Then came the reported Realme merger, the Smartprix report that OxygenOS would be folded into ColorOS, and finally OnePlus's own websites in Germany, Spain and France running banners pushing shoppers towards Oppo instead.Oppo will move into the space OnePlus leaves behind in Europe. There is an obvious flaw in that plan: Oppo phones cost more. You cannot fill a value-brand hole with a premium lineup and expect nobody to notice. Nothing is official until Oppo says it is—but the OnePlus 15 now looks like the brand's last major Western release, and a five-star one at that.
Article Summary: OnePlus is reportedly exiting the US and Europe, with India left as the brand's biggest surviving market. India accounts for well over half of OnePlus's annual sales, and the Nord series still sells hard in the mid-range. Remaining inventory in Europe and the US is being sold off.

Article Title: Moody’s chief economist Mark Zandi sees 'big warning' signs in June Jobs report for the US; says: Decline in unemployment rate was misleading because it coincided with a sharp drop in ...
Article Text:
Household survey weakness



Adjusted unemployment measure



Other economists weigh in



Mark Zandi, the chief economist of Moody’s Analytics has cautioned that the June employment report paints an overly optimistic picture of the US labour market. According to a report by Benzinga, in a series of posts shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) Zandi argued that commentary around the report was “much too dismissive of how weak the numbers looked, all the noise in the data notwithstanding. ” Zandi noted that payroll employment posted only modest gain in June, while in the months prior to June, job gains were revised downward. He further added that most of the hiring came from the healthcare sector rather than being broadly distributed across the economy.“Not only did employment as measured by the payroll survey post a small gain in the month, but previous month’s gains were revised much lower, and the bulk of the job gains were in healthcare. And employment as measured by the household survey fell sharply again, as it has all year,” wrote Zandi.The economist further pointed to the household survey, saying employment “fell sharply again, as it has all year.” He argued that the decline in the rate of unemployment was misleading because it coincided with a sharp drop in labour force participation. Participation has fallen across most demographic groups, particularly among workers under 35.“The unemployment rate ticked lower, but only because labor force participation is in free-fall. Participation is down across most demographic groups, especially among workers under 35. Employment-to-population ratio for prime-age workers also fell. The declines are surely overstated, but even so,” added Zandi.Zandi cited his “vicious-cycle measure,” which adjusts unemployment for trend labor force participation. He said the measure rose above 5% in June: “Without the outsize decline in participation, unemployment would be over 5%.”“You may recall our vicious-cycle measure, which adjusts the unemployment rate for trend labor force participation. It rose to over 5% in June. That is, without the outsize decline in participation, unemployment would be over 5%. As I said, the commentary on the June report was much too sanguine,” wrote Zandi in a post on X.Some economists echoed concerns about the June data. Laura Ullrich of Indeed Hiring Lab suggested the decline in participation may reflect a shrinking worker supply rather than weaker hiring demand, noting employers could still be seeking workers but facing fewer available candidates.Meanwhile, Cathie Wood of ARK Invest called the report “weird”, arguing government labor statistics appeared distorted due to differences between payroll and household surveys. She advocated using more private-sector data to assess labor market conditions.
Article Summary: Mark Zandi, the chief economist of Moody’s Analytics has cautioned that the June employment report paints an overly optimistic picture of the US labour market. Zandi argued that commentary around the report was “much too dismissive of how weak the numbers looked, all the noise in the data notwithstanding”

Article Title: Read the letter Eric Schmidt, Reid Hoffman, and top economists signed warning about AI wiping away millions of jobs; send a warning: Economists, policymakers and technology leaders must act now to und
Article Text:
Who all have signed the letter



What the letter says



Over 200 of the world’s most influential economists, technology executives and researchers have signed an open letter warning that artificial intelligence (AI) poses a serious and growing threat to jobs. The letter also says that the governments are not moving fast enough to prepare for what is coming. The letter, titled “We Must Act Now” and subtitled “A Statement on AI's Transformation of the Economy”, was organised by the Stanford Digital Economy Lab. At just 88 words, it is deliberately concise.Among those who signed: former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman, and Nobel Prize laureates Joseph Stiglitz, Daron Acemoglu, and Simon Johnson. Also on the list are Google AI lead Jeff Dean, Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark and OpenAI finance chief Sarah Friar — making it one of the rare documents that brings together both AI builders and the economists studying the technology's consequences. Other include Godfathers of AI Yoshua Bengio and Yann LeCun, and Vinod Khosla.The letter’s argument is straightforward: It warns that AI could become “radically more powerful” over the coming decade, and without meaningful action from policymakers, the result could be “large-scale job displacement” on a scale the world has not seen before.We Must Act NowA Statement on AI’s Transformation of the EconomyAI may become radically more powerful over the next 10 years.This could drive an unprecedented transformation of our economy, larger than the Industrial Revolution, but unfolding over a vastly shorter time frame. It could bring risks, including large-scale job displacement, as well as opportunities such as major gains in living standards.Economists, policymakers and technology leaders must act now to understand the economics of transformative AI and to build the incentives, guardrails, and institutions needed to steer AI in a direction that complements humans and benefits society.The letter comes as Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has predicted that AI could eliminate up to half of all entry-level white-collar jobs within five years. Many economists and technologists sit somewhere in between, arguing that AI is more likely to transform jobs than replace them outright.
Article Summary: Eric Schmidt, Reid Hoffman, Joseph Stiglitz, Daron Acemoglu, Simon Johnson, Jeff Dean, Sarah Friar, Yoshua Bengio and Yann LeCun all sign letter. Letter was organised by the Stanford Digital Economy Lab.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Steve Jobs’ widow Laurene Powell Jobs: "To do what you wanna do, to leave a mark, in a way that…" - a life well-lived is measured by what we leave behind
Article Text:
Laurene Powell Jobs (Image: Wikipedia)

Quote of the day by Laurene Powell Jobs

"To do what you wanna do, to leave a mark, in a way that you think is important and lasting, that's a life well-lived"

The deeper meaning of Laurene Powell Jobs’ quote

Where this reflection actually comes from

Why lasting impact has defined her own work since

A meaningful legacy is rarely built overnight

Personal success becomes richer when it benefits others

Other memorable quotes by Laurene Powell Jobs

"Regardless of zip code, talent and IQ are evenly distributed, so we need to make sure that opportunity is evenly distributed, too."

"Broken institutions are an opportunity rather than a time to go home."

"The innovation and creativity that's so manifest in the rest of society needs to be turned on our school systems."

"Whether someone signs something is not what's important. It's what they do and how they do it that matters."

Why this timeless message still resonates

Most people want their life to add up to more than a list of achievements. Laurene Powell Jobs put that idea into one sentence: "To do what you wanna do, to leave a mark, in a way that you think is important and lasting, that's a life well-lived. " It is a simple way of separating a full life from a merely busy one, built around what actually lasts rather than what looks impressive in the moment. The words are plain, almost conversational, yet they draw a clear line between chasing recognition and building something that continues to matter once the attention has moved on. It is the kind of definition that works just as well for a teacher or a small business owner as it does for anyone running a large philanthropic organisation.The quote opens with authenticity. Doing what you actually want to do, rather than following expectations set by someone else, is presented as the starting point, not an optional extra. Purpose cannot simply be copied from someone else's definition of success.The "mark" she describes is deliberately left open. It is not defined by wealth or fame. It could be a school, an idea, a piece of writing, or simply a life that quietly made things better for the people around it.The final phrase, "that's a life well-lived," shifts the whole measurement away from visibility and toward whether something genuinely lasting was actually built.Powell Jobs gave this interview only months after Steve Jobs ' death in October 2011, at a moment when a great deal of public attention was focused on his legacy specifically. Rather than talking only about her late husband's achievements, she used the interview to describe her own view of what makes a life meaningful, a definition built around lasting contribution rather than public recognition.That context matters. She was not offering a detached philosophy. She was speaking from inside a very public, very recent experience of watching someone's life get measured and remeasured by the world after it ended.Powell Jobs founded Emerson Collective, an organisation that blends philanthropy with policy work and investment across education, immigration and journalism, rather than operating as a conventional grant-making foundation. She has spoken about wanting talent and opportunity distributed as evenly as intelligence already is, and has described broken institutions as something worth rebuilding rather than abandoning.That approach mirrors the quote closely. Rather than chasing quick, visible wins, her work has consistently focused on slower, structural change in education and immigration policy, the kind of contribution that takes years to show results and rarely produces an immediate headline.Modern culture tends to celebrate sudden success, viral moments and instant recognition, which can create the impression that meaningful achievement happens quickly. Most lasting contributions do not work that way. Institutions, research and community change all tend to accumulate slowly, through effort that rarely draws attention while it is actually happening.What stands out in the quote is its outward focus. It is not simply about achieving something for yourself. It is about creating something that continues to matter to other people once your own involvement in it has ended, which turns individual ambition into something with a longer shelf life than personal achievement alone usually has.In a culture that constantly measures, compares and shares achievement, Powell Jobs' quote is a reminder that the value of a life rarely comes down to any of that. What tends to last is whatever was actually built for other people to use, long after the person who built it has moved on to something else.
Article Summary: Powell Jobs gave the quote only months after Steve Jobs'death in October 2011. She was speaking from inside a very public, very recent experience of watching someone's life get measured and remeasured by the world after it ended. Her work has consistently focused on slower, structural change in education and immigration.

Article Title: AI features and trust are key smartphone purchase drivers, finds CMR Study
Article Text:
AI-generated image for representational purpose

Smartphone purchase in India: Trust is non-negotiable



India seeing growing literacy around chipsets



AI has officially transitioned from a futuristic gimmick into one of the primary deciders for Indian smartphone buyers, with data privacy and experiential trust emerging as other critical factors driving next-generation purchases. According to the CMR Smartphone AI Pulse 2026 by CyberMedia Research (CMR), consumer expectations have fundamentally shifted.The report, which surveyed over 2,000 smartphone users aged 18–35 across eight major Indian cities, says that AI capabilities now rank in the top three defining attributes of a good smartphone, pushing ahead of traditional selling points like aesthetics, price and battery life. According to Prabhu Ram, VP, Industry Research Group (IRG), CyberMedia Research (CMR), “AI is no longer viewed as an added feature; it is increasingly shaping the overall device experience. ”“Across demographics and price segments, consumers expect AI that is useful, intuitive, and seamlessly integrated into everyday interactions. As these expectations evolve, AI capabilities will play a growing role in smartphone differentiation and purchase decisions going forward,” he added.As AI tools integrate deeper into daily life, Indian consumers are growing heavily conscious of how their personal data is handled.An 82% of respondents stated that transparent data practices are critical to building trust in smartphone AI. Furthermore, 61% of users believe that on-device AI processing (rather than cloud-based processing) is the ideal solution, noting that it drastically improves both device responsiveness and personal privacy.The study also highlights that AI engagement among Indian youth is deeply embedded, though distributed across different user habits. For example, 77% of consumers use AI-powered photography features, such as low-light enhancements and intelligent scene detection, making the camera the primary gateway to AI adoption.When it comes to generative AI, 71% of users engage with these tools multiple times a week for tasks like AI-assisted search, text summarization, live translation and writing support. Thirdly, while 57% of consumers fully understand and actively utilise their phone's AI suite, the remaining 43% engage only partially.The survey also exposed a clear generational and gender split. Gen Z leads the charge, with 72% stating AI is crucial for their next device purchase compared to 65% of Millennials. Meanwhile, 66% of female users prioritise camera and imaging AI features, whereas 42% of male users focus on productivity and communication tools.The report also pointed out that Indian consumers are becoming tech-literate, with 69% identifying the underlying chipset as the key enabler of smooth AI performance, gaming optimisation and battery efficiency. This awareness spikes significantly among Gen Z consumers at 83%.“The competitive battleground is moving from hardware specifications to experiential trust. Consumers increasingly evaluate AI experiences through the lens of trust, privacy, and real-world utility,” concluded Sourabh Pandey, an analyst at CMR.
Article Summary: AI capabilities now rank in the top three defining attributes of a good smartphone, pushing ahead of traditional selling points like aesthetics, price and battery life. Indian consumers are becoming tech-literate, with 69% identifying the underlying chipset as the key enabler of smooth AI performance and gaming optimisation.

Article Title: Waze rolls out Gemini-powered features including new motorcycle mode for riders
Article Text:
Waze's big Gemini update is here

Personalized navigation learns your driving habits

Gemini now handles reporting and destination search

Waze is rolling out five new features today, and the update leans hard into Google's Gemini push while also giving riders and daily commuters more control over how the app talks to them. The changes cover everything from motorcycle-specific routing to voice searches powered by AI, and they start hitting phones globally starting today.The biggest addition is Motorcycle mode, which uses AI to factor in two-wheeler shortcuts, road restrictions, and hazards like potholes, speed bumps, raised crosswalks, and narrow bridges—the stuff that barely registers for a car but can wreck a rider's day. It's backed by real-time traffic data and a dedicated team of motorcycle map editors, though the rollout is limited for now to Argentina, Brazil, Colombia, Malaysia, Mexico, Peru, and the Philippines, with more markets promised later.Waze will now suggest routes based on a user's past trips, not just live traffic patterns. So if you consistently pick highways over side streets with multiple stops, expect the app to surface that route first. Users who'd rather stick to Waze's standard ETA-first suggestions can pick alternate routes or switch personalization off entirely in settings. This one's rolling out worldwide on both Android and iOS.There's also a "Less chatty" mode for anyone tired of Waze interrupting a podcast every ninety seconds.It trims down voice prompts and keeps the ones that remain short, while still flagging hazards, turns, and lane changes when it actually matters.Conversational Reporting, which already let users flag slowdowns by talking naturally, now extends to map corrections—saying "the road is closed here" sends the update to local editors for verification. Meanwhile, Gemini-powered destination search lets users tap the voice icon and ask things like "find a gas station with the lowest prices nearby," with results ready to navigate to by voice. That last feature is currently limited to Waze's beta community.
Article Summary: Waze is rolling out five new features today, including motorcycle-specific routing and voice searches powered by AI. The update leans hard into Google's Gemini push while also giving riders and daily commuters more control over how the app talks to them. Waze will now suggest routes based on a user's past trips, not just traffic patterns.

Article Title: China is building an asteroid monitoring network that will use telescopes and satellites for planetary defence: Here’s how it will work
Article Text:
Representative Image

How China is planning to build a round-the-clock asteroid surveillance system

“No asteroid has so far been identified that will definitely collide with Earth in the foreseeable future, but concerns over impact risks are not unfounded.

Many near-Earth asteroids remain undetected.”

“We must never let our guard down, but there is also no need for excessive anxiety.”

China is developing a space-ground integrated monitoring and early-warning network as part of a planetary defence system, which is currently under feasibility study. According to a report by Chinese news agency Xinhua, Li Mingtao, chief scientist at the asteroid monitoring and early-warning research centre under the China National Space Administration (CNSA), said that the proposed system will combine ground-based telescopes with a space-based monitoring constellation to provide continuous surveillance of near-Earth asteroids.Mingtao announced the plan on International Asteroid Day, observed annually on June 30 to raise awareness about asteroid impact risks and planetary defence. He said the network is designed to eliminate monitoring blind spots by coordinating observations from Earth and space.According to Mingtao, China will deploy multiple large-aperture optical telescopes at carefully selected sites to create a geographically distributed observation network capable of conducting long-range, wide-area night-sky surveys.To address the limitations of ground-based telescopes, which cannot observe objects near the Sun because of atmospheric scattering and sunlight, China also plans to launch a space-based monitoring constellation. The satellites will monitor asteroids approaching from the sunward direction, enabling continuous observations regardless of weather or daylight conditions.Mingtao said,He added,According to the scientist, more than 40,000 near-Earth asteroids have already been discovered and catalogued globally, but many smaller or faint objects remain undetected.China has also made initial progress in developing risk assessment models and algorithms and is building an operational near-Earth asteroid early-warning system. Once a telescope identifies a potential object of concern, the system will automatically calculate its orbit and estimate the probability of an impact on Earth.Li said that if a credible and urgent threat is confirmed, authorities will be notified immediately, and the public will be informed of the potential risk and recommended actions.The scientist also outlined two possible approaches to planetary defence if an asteroid is found to be on a collision course with Earth. The first is a kinetic impact mission, in which a spacecraft strikes the asteroid at high speed to alter its orbit. The second includes techniques such as gravity tractors, ion beams and laser ablation, which require significantly more advanced warning to be effective.Mingtao says the biggest hurdle is still detecting the unknown near-Earth asteroids, especially those coming from the direction of the Sun. This makes ongoing surveillance and early warning systems a priority for planetary defence work.
Article Summary: China is developing a space-ground integrated monitoring and early-warning network as part of a planetary defence system. The network is designed to eliminate monitoring blind spots by coordinating observations from Earth and space. Once a telescope identifies a potential object of concern, the system will automatically calculate its orbit and estimate the probability of an impact.

Article Title: Quote of the day by BlackRock CEO Larry Fink: To finance longer life spans, we must convince individuals to …
Article Text:
"To finance longer life spans, we must convince individuals to start investing now for the long term.

But longevity should be an asset that can be leveraged, not a curse. They must understand that there's a cost to sitting in cash.

No one talks about that cost."

What Larry Fink's quote means



Investing isn't just about returns: Larry Fink



BlackRock CEO Larry Fink believes people need to start investing earlier to be financially prepared for longer lives. He said,His message is that simply saving money is not always enough. Investing for the long term can help people build wealth that keeps pace with rising costs and longer retirements.People are living longer than previous generations, which means they may need their savings to last for decades after they stop working. Larry Fink argues that investing early gives money more time to grow through compounding, making it easier to build a larger retirement fund over time.He also cautions against holding too much cash for long periods. Cash seems safe, but inflation can erode its purchasing power over the years. In the past, investments like stocks, bonds, or diversified mutual funds have provided better long-term growth opportunities, but they also involve risk, and their values can go up and down.According to Larry Fink, planning for the future includes considering both safety and growth. Investment plans should be made with considerations such as goals, the amount of money a person will save, the level of risk a person is willing to bear, how long a person will invest, and a backup plan for emergencies, rather than just trying to save money.Some people would like to have more money in cash, while others would prefer to invest more and gain from it. According to Larry Fink, his statement is a reminder that people need to think about more than just saving money nowadays. It will become much easier to spend a longer period of time when a person starts investing early.
Article Summary: Investing for the long term can help people build wealth that keeps pace with rising costs and longer retirements. Larry Fink argues that investing early gives money more time to grow through compounding. Cash seems safe, but inflation can erode its purchasing power over the years.

Article Title: Humanoid robots complete first-ever live surgical procedure under surgeons' control, researchers say clinical challenges remain
Article Text:

Researchers evaluate humanoid robots for future surgical care



“Humanoid form factors offer unique potential, particularly for assisting with surgical tasks.

Traditionally, robotic systems for surgery are purpose-built platforms such as Intuitive Surgical's da Vinci Surgical System, and it remains unclear how close current humanoid systems are to meeting the precision, control, and safety requirements of minimally invasive surgery."

Researchers at the University of California, San Diego, have used two humanoid robots to perform a live gallbladder removal surgery on a pig. This marks what the team describes as the first time humanoid robots have completed such a procedure on a living patient. The surgery was carried out with the robots being fully teleoperated by trained human surgeons, while researchers evaluated whether general-purpose humanoid robots could eventually help extend surgical care to locations with limited access to specialists.The procedure involved laparoscopic cholecystectomy, in which the robots retracted tissue, dissected, applied clips and removed the gallbladder. According to the researchers, the robots remained under continuous human control throughout the operation, and several technical challenges still need to be addressed before the technology can be used in clinical settings.The study was conducted by researchers from the University of California, San Diego School of Medicine and the university's Advanced Robotics and Controls Laboratory (ARClab). Rather than developing a custom-built surgical robot, the team used two commercially available Unitree G1 humanoid robots, which were modified for the experiment.In a GitHub overview of the project, the researchers wrote,The researchers reported that the robots successfully completed the surgical procedure on living tissue. However, a paper published in Nature noted that there are stillThe Unitree G1 robots used in the study are commercially available humanoid robots that stand around four to five feet tall and weigh about 70 pounds. According to the researchers, the systems were equipped with dexterous robotic hands, wrist articulation and depth-sensing technology to manipulate surgical instruments. During the procedure, the robots were also tethered as a safety measure to prevent accidental movement.The researchers said humanoid robots could eventually be used in environments where access to surgeons is limited, including rural hospitals and remote locations. Unlike purpose-built surgical robots that remain fixed in operating rooms, humanoid robots are designed to move through human-built spaces and perform various physical tasks while being operated remotely by medical specialists.
Article Summary: Researchers at the University of California, San Diego, have used two humanoid robots to perform a live gallbladder removal surgery on a pig. This marks what the team describes as the first time humanoid robots have completed such a procedure on a living patient. The robots remained under continuous human control throughout the operation, and several technical challenges still need to be addressed before the technology can be used in clinical settings.

Article Title: How AI could make big buildings use 42% to 48% less energy, while keeping comfort steady and indoor air cleaner in real-world style tests
Article Text:
Traditional building-control systems often operate through fixed schedules, rules or discrete time intervals, but real buildings do not behave in neat steps | ChatGPT

Traditional building-control systems often operate through fixed schedules, rules or discrete time intervals, but real buildings do not behave in neat steps | ChatGPT

An AI system designed to follow buildings as they change

The tests drew on a large archive of actual building data

The new NODE-RL-BEM framework goes beyond prediction by connecting continuous-time modeling with adaptive control | ChatGPT

The savings are promising, but deployment is the next test

Heating, cooling and ventilating large buildings involves a constant balancing act: reducing energy consumption can conflict with keeping occupants comfortable and maintaining healthy indoor air, while changing weather, occupancy and equipment use make a building’s behavior difficult to predict from one hour to the next. A new artificial intelligence framework now suggests those competing demands could be managed together, with tests reporting energy savings of 42% to 48%, comfort violations below 0.5%, and improvements in indoor air quality of 28% to 35%. The system, called NODE-RL-BEM, combines neural ordinary differential equations with reinforcement learning, allowing the AI to model how a building changes continuously over time while learning which control decisions are most effective. According to the study published in Scientific Reports , the framework was evaluated using the ASHRAE Great Energy Predictor III dataset and an Intelligent Indoor Environment Dataset, rather than through a live deployment across occupied buildings, meaning the results represent data-driven, real-world-style testing rather than a confirmed 48% reduction in an operational building.Traditional building-control systems often operate through fixed schedules, rules or discrete time intervals, but real buildings do not behave in neat steps. Outdoor temperature changes continuously, people enter and leave rooms, air quality shifts, and heating or cooling demand can rise unexpectedly, creating a highly dynamic system in which a decision that worked earlier may no longer be efficient.NODE-RL-BEM attempts to solve that problem by learning the building’s changing state continuously and pairing that model with reinforcement learning, which allows the system to improve control decisions according to multiple objectives rather than optimizing energy consumption alone. The researchers report that this approach produced smoother state predictions and adaptive responses to changing environmental and occupancy conditions, while achieving a generalization score of 0.91 across different operational scenarios. That ability to transfer performance between different conditions is particularly important because large building portfolios can contain offices, educational facilities, and other properties with very different energy-use patterns, equipment, and occupancy schedules.One of the key datasets behind the evaluation has its origins in a major effort to collect real energy-meter readings from non-residential buildings. According to the Building Data Genome Project 2 study in Scientific Data , the wider dataset contains information from 3,053 energy meters across 1,636 non-residential buildings, covering two full years of hourly measurements from sites in North America and Europe, including electricity, heating, cooling, steam, and other meter data. Part of this information was used in the ASHRAE Great Energy Predictor III competition, giving researchers a large and heterogeneous foundation for testing whether machine-learning systems can handle the variability found across actual buildings.According to the original ASHRAE Great Energy Predictor III competition study , the competition itself involved thousands of participants working with millions of building-energy data points, underscoring the scale and complexity of predicting energy use across diverse properties. The new NODE-RL-BEM framework goes beyond prediction by connecting continuous-time modeling with adaptive control, attempting to determine not only what a building is likely to do next, but how its systems should respond.The reported 42% to 48% energy savings are substantial, particularly because the model simultaneously kept comfort violations below 0.5% and reported better indoor air quality, but the distinction between dataset-based evaluation and live building deployment remains important. The study demonstrates what the framework achieved under its experimental evaluation conditions; it does not yet establish that every office tower, hospital, or university building could immediately cut energy consumption by nearly half.What the research does show is that AI-based building control may be able to treat energy, comfort, and air quality as interconnected objectives rather than forcing facility managers to optimize one at the expense of another. The next major step will be demonstrating whether those gains remain stable when the system is connected to real HVAC equipment, unpredictable occupants, and the operational constraints of buildings running around the clock.
Article Summary: NODE-RL-BEM combines neural ordinary differential equations with reinforcement learning. It models how a building changes continuously over time while learning which control decisions are most effective. Tests reported energy savings of 42% to 48%, comfort violations below 0.5%, and improvements in indoor air quality of 28% to 35%.

Article Title: European Union rules that Meta's Instagram and Facebook are 'addictive' by design; threatens millions of dollar as fine; company responds 'angrily': We disagree as these findings don't...
Article Text:
EU finds Meta's Instagram, Facebook design 'addictive'; company faces fine up to 6% of global revenue

Meta downplayed how much time teens spend on the apps at night, Commission says

Meta disagrees with the findings, points to its Teen Accounts safeguards

This is Meta's second DSA finding this year, after the under-13 ruling in April

Brussels has run out of patience with the scroll. The European Commission said on July 10 that it has preliminarily found Meta in breach of the Digital Services Act, concluding that Instagram and Facebook were built to keep people hooked rather than simply engaged.The list of culprits is familiar: infinite scroll, autoplay, push notifications, and recommendation feeds tuned to know exactly what keeps a thumb moving. The ruling wraps up a two year investigation into what that design does to users' mental and physical wellbeing, with minors and vulnerable adults singled out as most at risk.The Commission's language is unusually blunt for a regulator—it says these features tip users' brains into "autopilot mode." Its prescription is just as direct: turn off autoplay and infinite scroll by default, introduce real screen time breaks, and stop optimising the recommender system purely for engagement.Should the findings stand once Meta has had its say, the company could be fined up to 6% of its global annual turnover, a figure that could top $12 billion based on last year's revenue.The Commission's core complaint is that Meta never seriously interrogated its own product decisions.Investigators say the company sat on data showing how many hours teenagers were logging on Instagram and Facebook after dark, and looked past how formats like Reels and Stories nudge people toward excessive use.Meta's existing guardrails didn't impress regulators either. Time management prompts, even the ones turned on by default for teen accounts, take one tap to dismiss and barely move usage numbers, the findings note.Parental controls come with the same catch: they only work if a parent has the technical fluency and spare time to actually configure them.Meta isn't conceding the point. Spokesperson Ben Walters said the findings overlook changes the company has already made, citing Teen Accounts that let parents block Instagram at night and cap daily screen time at 15 minutes.The company says it plans to keep talking to Brussels rather than dig in. That's less about goodwill than procedure—Meta now gets to review the Commission's case files and submit a formal rebuttal before anything becomes binding. A fine, if it comes, is still months away.Friday's findings aren't an isolated jab. The Commission dinged Meta in April for failing to keep under-13s off its platforms, and it's separately probing so called "rabbit hole" effects, where recommendation algorithms steer young users toward increasingly extreme content over time.TikTok faced near identical charges in February. The timing here is no accident, either: an EU expert panel briefs Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on Monday with recommendations on child safety online, feeding into a broader push—already gaining ground in France—toward an Australia style social media ban for teenagers across the bloc.
Article Summary: EU finds Meta's Instagram, Facebook design 'addictive'; company faces fine up to 6% of global revenue. Commission says these features tip users' brains into "autopilot mode" Meta disagrees with the findings, points to its Teen Accounts safeguards.

Article Title: Why Russia's NATO doorbell camera hack is a warning for every smart home owner
Article Text:
AI image for representational purpose

How hackers ‘broke into’ digital cameras



Camera hacking : A growing war tactic



How to lock down your smart cameras



Turn on auto-updates

Change the factory password

Audit app access

Shield your home Wi-Fi network

Create a ‘guest network’

Keep the router updated

Russia spied on Nato military bases through civilian cameras connected to the internet, and monitored the transfer of military equipment to Ukraine, according to AIVD domestic security and MIVD military intelligence agencies in the Netherlands. According to a joint investigation by the domestic security (AIVD) and military intelligence (MIVD) agencies, the hackers systematically targeted cameras facing critical infrastructure across European NATO member states, including the Netherlands, as well as inside Ukraine. The goal of the operation was also to identify exactly what types of weapons are being shipped to Kyiv – Capital of Ukraine.Officials confirmed that the targeted organisations and homeowners along these strategic military routes have now been warned so they can take immediate defensive action.The rise of internet-connected smart cameras and doorbell systems has made home monitoring highly accessible for everyday consumers. However, these same conveniences have created massive vulnerabilities.Intelligence agencies pointed out that the operation was able to succeed because a vast majority of these civilian devices are unsecured. Hackers rely on readily available apps to scan the web for accessible devices, easily breaking in because the cameras frequently rely on “standard factory passwords, outdated software (firmware) and basic default configurations.”“When the IP camera is identified, the malicious party can attempt to access the IP camera via the internet. This is often relatively easy, because many IP cameras connected to the internet are insufficiently secure,” the agencies said.In easier words, once an unsecured camera is located, foreign operatives can easily look through its lens from halfway across the world – just like you may have seen in spy movies. A report by the Telegraph, using civilian property cameras has quickly become a preferred tactic in modern warfare because it is significantly cheaper and easier than deploying military drones or spy satellites.Furthermore, what makes these ground-based cameras unique is that they offer a close-up perspective of the terrain that aerial photography cannot match – while the device owners remain unaware they are being used as digital scouts.This is not the first time that everyday security tech has been weaponised. Ukrainian hackers have previously hijacked Russian street and home surveillance cameras to track enemy troop movements and successfully coordinate long-range drone strikes.More recently, reports claimed that Israeli security officials warned that Iran has used private security cameras to locate targets for drone and missile barrages. Conversely, there have been reports saying that forced their way into a massive network of traffic and security cameras across Tehran to locate and track high-level targets before launching decisive air strikes.You have a choice not to be a military target and protect your privacy. Tech experts and security agencies have recommend taking these easy steps to ensure your cameras aren't being watched by strangers.Hackers actively hunt for security bugs in old device code. Enabling automatic firmware updates ensures your camera always has the latest security patches.Never leave a smart camera on its default setting, and create a strong, unique password immediately upon setup. If you have given your password to repairman, change it immediately.If you gave temporary account or app access to a former roommate, landlord or family member, remove their permissions when no longer needed.Change your home Wi-Fi network name (SSID) so it does not reveal the brand of your router or the name of your internet service provider.If possible, set up a separate ‘Guest’ Wi-Fi network on your router and connect all your smart home gadgets, including doorbell cameras, smart bulbs, and TVs, to it. This will keep your smart devices isolated from the main network where you store personal data, computers and financial information.Just like your cameras, ensure your main home router is running the latest software updates to seal up hidden security holes.
Article Summary: Russia spied on Nato military bases through civilian cameras connected to the internet, according to AIVD domestic security and MIVD military intelligence agencies in the Netherlands. The hackers systematically targeted cameras facing critical infrastructure across European NATO member states, including the Netherlands, as well as inside Ukraine. The goal of the operation was also to identify exactly what types of weapons are being shipped to Kyiv.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Bill Gates: "Success is a lousy teacher. It seduces smart people into…" - a powerful reminder that failure often teaches the lessons success never can
Article Text:
Co-Founder of Microsoft Bill Gates

Quote of the day by Bill Gates

"Success is a lousy teacher. It seduces smart people into thinking they can't lose"

The deeper meaning of Bill Gates’ quotes

Where this quote by Bill Gates actually comes from

Why failure often teaches what success cannot

Confidence with humility attached

Other memorable quotes by Bill Gates

"Your most unhappy customers are your greatest source of learning."

"It's fine to celebrate success, but it is more important to heed the lessons of failure ."

"We all need people who will give us feedback. That's how we improve."

Why this still matters today

Most people assume success is the best proof that they are doing something right. Bill Gates argued almost the opposite. "Success is a lousy teacher," he wrote. "It seduces smart people into thinking they can't lose." Coming from someone who co-founded one of the most dominant technology companies in history, that is a striking thing to admit, and it carries more weight because he wrote it while Microsoft was sitting right at the top of its industry. Nearly three decades later, the warning has aged well, since Microsoft itself went on to miss exactly the kind of shift the quote seems to have been anticipating, in a way few companies at the height of their power ever manage to predict about themselves.Most people assume success proves their decisions were correct. Gates is arguing the opposite is often closer to the truth. When things keep going well, people stop questioning their own methods, because there is no obvious reason to. That confidence can quietly harden into something closer to arrogance, a growing certainty that future decisions will also work out, simply because past ones did.Calling success a "lousy teacher" is a specific claim. Victory tends to hide weak decisions rather than expose them.Someone can succeed despite a flawed process, and never notice the flaw until circumstances change and the same weak decision finally fails. Intelligence does not protect against this either. If anything, capable people may be more vulnerable to it, since a long run of good outcomes reinforces the belief that their judgement is always sound.Gates wrote this in The Road Ahead, his 1995 book about technology and the future, published at a moment when Microsoft dominated personal computing almost completely. Even from that position of obvious strength, he was already warning against the exact trap that dominance can create.The warning turned out to be well-timed. Microsoft went on to badly underestimate the importance of internet search, leaving room for Google to take over that market entirely, and it later struggled to compete once Apple's iPhone and Android reshaped mobile computing. Gates has spoken openly about both setbacks rather than downplaying them, treating them as evidence of the exact pattern his own quote had already described.Failure forces a specific kind of question that success rarely does. What went wrong. Which assumption turned out to be false. What would need to change next time. Success, by contrast, tends to prompt celebration rather than scrutiny, which means weak points can stay hidden long after they should have been addressed.This pattern shows up well beyond business. Scientists refine theories after failed experiments. Athletes study losses more closely than wins. In every case, failure hands over information that a smooth run of success simply does not generate on its own.Confidence is what gets people to take a risk or launch something new in the first place. Left unchecked, though, it can slide into certainty, and certainty stops people asking the questions that kept them sharp in the first place. Humility is the counterweight, the habit of assuming markets, technology and circumstances will keep shifting regardless of how well things have gone so far.Gates' quote is really pointing at that balance. Success deserves to be enjoyed. It should never become a reason to stop paying attention.Social media makes success look effortless, showcasing the win while hiding the years of setbacks that came before it. That creates a quiet, false impression that people who succeed rarely get things wrong.Gates' quote pushes back against exactly that impression. Lasting success depends less on avoiding failure altogether and more on staying genuinely teachable once success actually arrives. Every achievement, in his framing, is a starting point for the next question, not proof that the questions are finished.
Article Summary: Most people assume success is the best proof that they are doing something right. Bill Gates argued almost the opposite. "Success is a lousy teacher. It seduces smart people into thinking they can't lose," he wrote in 1995. Microsoft went on to badly underestimate the importance of internet search, leaving room for Google to take over that market.

Article Title: 'The world wants me to die': Bryan Johnson says people are celebrating his Autoimmune Gastritis diagnosis because he challenged death
Article Text:
Bryan Johnson says diagnosis sparked a wave of online backlash



Why Bryan Johnson believes people wanted him to fail



Bryan Johnson points to Gilgamesh, Asclepius and Jesus



Bryan Johnson says people expect anyone who challenges death to fail



His view of the future



A message for supporters



Bryan Johnson has responded at length to the intense reaction that followed his recent health disclosure, arguing that the public response revealed far more than attitudes towards his personal circumstances. The technology entrepreneur, known for spending millions on longevity research and health monitoring, said his diagnosis with Autoimmune Gastritis quickly became an international talking point, drawing thousands of news reports and widespread discussion across social media. While many supporters expressed concern, he believes a sizeable share of the online conversation celebrated the news rather than sympathised with it.In a detailed statement published on X (Formerly Twitter), Johnson suggested that this response stemmed from long-standing ideas about mortality and humanity's relationship with death. His comments, which attracted more than 1.2 million views within hours, have reignited debate around both his health and the broader philosophy behind his anti-ageing work.Johnson said he did not expect the announcement to spread so quickly, describing the coverage as almost impossible to avoid in the days after revealing his condition.According to him, the news travelled rapidly across social media platforms before being picked up by hundreds of publications around the world.Among the supportive messages, he also noticed a different response. He claimed many online comments suggested that his illness was somehow ‘deserved’ because he has spent years publicly questioning accepted ideas about ageing and extending human life. Rather than seeing those reactions as isolated insults, he believes they reflected something more deeply rooted in how people respond to challenges to long-held beliefs.Johnson rejected the idea that the response could be explained solely by people enjoying another person's misfortune. Instead, he argued that individuals often feel more comfortable when someone who challenges accepted thinking appears to fail.In his view, questioning the inevitability of death forces people to confront assumptions they have accepted throughout their lives. If those assumptions begin to look uncertain, he suggested, it can create discomfort. Seeing the challenger encounter setbacks may therefore restore a sense of certainty rather than simply providing entertainment.He pointed to comments saying he "deserved it" as an example of this pattern, suggesting that the criticism was directed not only at him but also at the ideas he represents.To explain his thinking, Johnson turned to several well-known historical and religious narratives that centre on humanity's pursuit of life beyond death.He referred to the ancient Epic of Gilgamesh, in which the central figure searches for eternal life after experiencing profound loss, only to see that possibility slip away. He also mentioned Asclepius from Greek mythology, whose ability to restore life was ultimately halted by Zeus.Johnson extended the comparison to the story of Jesus, arguing that each narrative follows a similar pattern in which someone who challenges accepted limits on life is eventually rejected or defeated. He acknowledged that comparing his own work with figures from mythology and religion would inevitably draw criticism, but maintained that the recurring themes remain relevant.Johnson argued that societies often reinforce existing beliefs by expecting anyone who questions them to be proven wrong. In his words, people need the challenger to lose because it protects their own understanding of reality.He suggested that accepting death as unavoidable allows people to make sense of both personal mortality and the deaths of loved ones. If that assumption were removed, he believes many established ideas about life would become harder to reconcile.Johnson said this pattern has existed for thousands of years, even if the language and cultural setting have changed over time.Although he acknowledged that death has shaped human thought throughout history, Johnson argued that advances in science have created circumstances unlike those faced by previous generations.He suggested that, for the first time, it may eventually become possible for physical death to be treated as something other than an unavoidable outcome. His statement ended with two questions directed at readers, asking whether he truly deserved the reaction he received and whether people might instead see him as someone working towards a shared goal rather than threatening established beliefs.As discussion around the statement continued, Johnson posted a follow-up message beneath the original thread. He encouraged followers not to view his diagnosis as a reason for sadness and thanked those who had offered support through public messages and private conversations.He said the diagnosis had strengthened rather than weakened his determination, describing it as a challenge he was prepared to face. Johnson also said he remained optimistic about future medical progress and appreciated those who continue to share his interest in extending healthy human life.
Article Summary: Bryan Johnson says people expect anyone who challenges death to fail. The technology entrepreneur said his diagnosis with Autoimmune Gastritis quickly became an international talking point. He believes a sizeable share of the online conversation celebrated the news rather than sympathised with it. He suggested that this response stemmed from long-standing ideas about mortality and humanity's relationship with death.

Article Title: TCS takes on OpenAI, Anthropic, Amazon and Microsoft; to build a team of forward-deployed engineers; CEO K Krithivasan says: We would be ensuring ...

Tata Consultancy Services ( TCS ) is building a team of up to 8,900 forward-deployed engineers as it expands its artificial intelligence (AI) business. The move puts India's largest IT services company in direct competition with firms such as OpenAI , Anthropic, Microsoft and Amazon , which are also hiring engineers to help customers adopt AI. As per a Reuters report, the company is also looking at acquisitions in AI, data security and cybersecurity. TCS CEO K Krithivasan said the company wants 1% to 1.5% of its workforce to become forward-deployed engineers (FDEs). "We would be ... ensuring that we have as many as 1% to 1.5% of our associates who could be what you would call FDEs," Krithivasan said.Based on TCS' workforce at the end of June, this would mean around 5,900 to 8,900 employees. He did not say whether the company would hire new employees or retrain its existing staff.For those unaware, forward-deployed engineers work closely with customers to speed up AI adoption. They help businesses customise AI tools and integrate them into existing systems.Besides expanding its engineering team, TCS is evaluating acquisitions in AI, cybersecurity and data security. The company has mostly relied on organic growth in the past and has avoided large acquisitions.“We are looking at where we can find things which will help us enable or enhance our strategic positioning,” TCS CFO Samir Seksaria said as quoted by Reuters.K Krithivasan also dismissed concerns that AI would weaken the outsourcing industry. He said companies will still need partners like TCS to connect AI models with their existing systems and manage data across their businesses.“What you need is a deep knowledge of the customer environment to make it work. That is where we differentiate ourselves. This has nothing to do with cost arbitrage. It's essentially because of the talent pool that we have built,” he said.He also said businesses are increasingly using multiple AI models, making integration work more important.
Article Summary: TCS is building a team of up to 8,900 forward-deployed engineers as it expands its artificial intelligence (AI) business. Article Title: Polymatech starts sapphire crystal production in Chennai to build local semiconductor materials capability
Article Text: Polymatech Electronics Limited has commissioned a sapphire ingot crystal-growth puller—an industrial crystal-growth furnace used to manufacture large blocks of single-crystal sapphire—at its Oragadam campus near Chennai, as part of the company's plan to expand its semiconductor materials manufacturing capabilities in India.The company said the furnace is designed to grow a 100 mm diameter sapphire ingot in five working days, with each ingot yielding a usable length of about 330 mm after cutting and grinding. Once qualified, the ingots are processed through slicing, grinding, lapping and polishing into epi-ready wafers. At full capacity, a single puller is expected to produce around 18,000 epi-ready sapphire wafers a year, which it said could translate into several billion semiconductor dies annually for micro-scale devices.The puller is currently undergoing process qualification and operational validation, during which parameters such as power quality, ultra-pure water supply, process gases and thermal conditions are being tested for consistent sapphire crystal growth.The Oragadam facility will serve as the baseline for the next phase of expansion, with additional sapphire ingot pullers to be set up at the company's SEZ at Nava Raipur in Chhattisgarh.The Nava Raipur SEZ spans 10.13 hectares and has been approved by the Ministry of Commerce and Industry for the manufacture of semiconductors and electronic components.The company said the India expansion will add to its existing sapphire ingot and wafer operations in Grenoble and France, and part of its broader manufacturing footprint across India, Singapore, France, Estonia and the US.Polymatech said the sapphire programme, like its other facilities, has been funded through the group's internal resources. The company works across semiconductor packaging, opto-electronics and advanced materials. The wider Polymatech Group's operations include LED chip-on-board packaging, memory modules, sapphire ingot and wafer production, semiconductor substrates, printed circuit boards, and test and reliability equipment.
Article Summary: The furnace is designed to grow a 100 mm diameter sapphire ingot in five working days. At full capacity, a single puller is expected to produce around 18,000 epi-ready wafers a year. This could translate into several billion semiconductor dies annually for micro-scale devices.

Article Title: Kellton Tech forms JV with Kuwait’s Action Energy for GCC energy digitisation
Article Text: Kellton Tech EU Limited, a wholly-owned subsidiary of Kellton Tech Solutions Limited, has entered into a joint venture with Kuwait's Action Energy Company K.S.C.P. (AEC) to offer digital and AI-based services to energy companies in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) region.According to the terms of the JV, AEC will hold a 51% stake while Kellton Tech EU will hold the remaining 49%. The JV has an initial term of five years, which will be renewed for successive three-year periods. It will initially operate across GCC countries, with the venture planning to open an office in Doha, Qatar, as its first step outside Kuwait, ahead of a proposed expansion into Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Oman.The joint venture will operate in two segments. Oil and gas, where it will offer digital oilfield solutions including Kellton's Optima platform, and information technology, spanning enterprise software, cloud computing, cybersecurity, ERP implementation, systems integration and managed services.Optima is Kellton's digital oilfield platform for workflow automation, asset performance monitoring and real-time visibility for field operations. The company said the platform will be deployed in combination with AEC's operational experience and its existing relationship with Kuwait Oil Company (KOC).The venture aims to combine the Kellton’s technology capabilities with AEC's presence in the local market, in order to help energy companies in the region modernise their operations and improve efficiency.According to an AEC spokesperson, the addressable market for oil and gas digitalisation in the GCC is estimated at over $1 billion annually, and that the company aims to capture at least 5% of this market over time.Kellton Tech EU Limited has more than 2,000 employees across North America, Europe, the Middle East and Asia. AEC provides integrated upstream oilfield services in Kuwait, including drilling, workover and well-related services.
Article Summary: Kellton Tech EU Limited has entered into a joint venture with Kuwait's Action Energy Company K.S.C. (AEC) The JV will offer digital and AI-based services to energy companies in the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) region. It will initially operate across GCC countries, with the venture planning to open an office in Qatar.

Article Title: Mark Zuckerberg's vintage $2 million Rolex from the 1950s isn't just a luxury watch, it tracks the Moon's cycles and is one of only two models ever made with this feature
Article Text:
Why is Mark Zuckerberg's $2 million vintage Rolex so special?









How does the moonphase feature work?

What else can the watch do?

Why is it worth around $2 million?

Mark Zuckerberg’s discussion while wearing the watch

Zuckerberg's growing collection of rare watches

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg recently caught the attention of watch enthusiasts after appearing with a rare vintage Rolex estimated to be worth around $2 million. While the conversation focused on how artificial intelligence could accelerate scientific and medical research, many viewers noticed the timepiece on his wrist instead. The watch, a Rolex Reference 6062 "Stelline" from the early 1950s, is far more than a luxury accessory. It combines a moonphase display, a triple calendar and an automatic movement in a design regarded as one of Rolex's greatest achievements. Produced in limited numbers for only a short period, the model has become one of the most sought-after vintage Rolex watches among collectors worldwide.The Rolex Reference 6062, commonly known as the "Stelline" because of its distinctive star-shaped hour markers, was introduced around 1950 during what many collectors consider Rolex's golden era. Unlike most Rolex watches of its time, which focused on durability and everyday wear, the 6062 showcased the brand's ability to create highly complicated mechanical timepieces. It was produced in yellow gold, pink gold and stainless steel variants, with precious metal models being especially rare and valuable today.One of the biggest reasons for its legendary status is that the Reference 6062 is one of only two Rolex references ever made to combine an automatic self-winding movement, a triple calendar and a moonphase complication in a single wristwatch.The other model, the Reference 8171, featured a larger case and a different design. This combination has made the 6062 one of the most celebrated achievements in Rolex's history.The moonphase display is one of the watch's most fascinating complications. A rotating disc beneath the dial illustrates the changing phases of the Moon, including the New Moon, First Quarter, Full Moon and Last Quarter. The mechanism completes a cycle roughly every 29.5 days, closely matching the Moon's natural lunar cycle.Before the digital age, moonphase displays had practical uses in navigation, astronomy and even agriculture, where lunar cycles were used to plan certain activities. Today, they are admired primarily for their mechanical complexity and the craftsmanship required to incorporate them into a wristwatch.Beyond displaying the time, the Rolex 6062 also features a triple calendar, showing the day of the week, the date and the month. It is powered by Rolex's automatic self-winding movement, allowing it to wind itself through the natural motion of the wearer's wrist.Combining all these functions in a relatively compact wristwatch during the early 1950s was an extraordinary technical accomplishment. At a time when many mechanical watches offered only basic timekeeping, the Reference 6062 demonstrated Rolex's expertise in producing sophisticated complications without compromising reliability or elegance.The value of the Rolex Reference 6062 is driven by a combination of rarity, historical importance and demand among collectors. Production lasted only a few years, leaving a relatively small number of surviving examples. Watches retaining their original dial, movement, hands and case are particularly prized because untouched examples have become increasingly difficult to find.Auction prices can vary widely depending on the watch's condition, metal, originality and documented ownership history, with exceptional examples selling for well over $2 million. Among vintage Rolex collectors, the 6062 is widely regarded as a "grail watch" because of its scarcity and significance in the brand's history.Zuckerberg wore the vintage Rolex during an appearance on the No Priors podcast alongside his wife, Priscilla Chan. The discussion focused on the growing role of artificial intelligence in scientific research, particularly its ability to analyse complex biological data, generate new scientific hypotheses and accelerate discoveries in medicine.The conversation also highlighted Meta's broader efforts in AI-powered science through initiatives aimed at helping researchers better understand cells, proteins and diseases. Zuckerberg suggested that increasingly capable AI systems could significantly reduce the time required for certain stages of biomedical research, potentially speeding up the development of new treatments.For much of his career, Zuckerberg was known for wearing simple grey T-shirts paired with inexpensive digital watches, including Casio models. In recent years, however, he has developed a noticeable interest in haute horology, building a collection that includes some of the world's most desirable mechanical timepieces.His collection reportedly features watches from Rolex, Patek Philippe, F.P. Journe, Greubel Forsey and De Bethune. Among the most talked-about pieces are the Greubel Forsey Hand Made 1, the Patek Philippe 5236P In-Line Perpetual Calendar and now the Rolex Reference 6062 "Stelline". The shift has attracted attention not only because of the watches' value but also because many are considered milestones in modern or vintage watchmaking, reflecting an appreciation for engineering and craftsmanship rather than luxury alone.
Article Summary: Zuckerberg wore the Rolex Reference 6062 "Stelline" during an appearance on the No Priors podcast alongside his wife, Priscilla Chan. The watch combines a moonphase display, a triple calendar and an automatic movement in a design regarded as one of Rolex's greatest achievements. Production lasted only a few years, leaving a relatively small number of surviving examples.

Article Title: Meet Zhenghua Yang: The game studio founder who recovered after he was told he has three hours to live at 18, and went on to built a $10 million-a-year game studio that started from hospital bed
Article Text:
PC: YouTube (TEDx Talks)

How Zhenghua Yang's life-threatening illness became the foundation of Serenity Forge

The $1,000 investment that started Serenity Forge

A business philosophy shaped outside the gaming industry

Why Zhenghua Yang turned down games worth millions

Players who shared personal stories

His view on building a business

University was only just beginning when Zhenghua Yang's plans were interrupted by a medical emergency that would reshape the course of his life. Instead of settling into lectures and campus routines, then,18-year-old found himself spending long periods in hospital after a rare blood disorder left him fighting for survival. Recovery stretched over months and then years, bringing repeated hospital visits and long periods away from the life he had expected to build. During those difficult days, video games became far more than entertainment. They offered routine, distraction, and a connection to the outside world at a time when very little felt normal. Years later, those experiences would become the foundation of a business that approaches game development with a different purpose, placing emotional impact ahead of commercial trends while still growing into a company generating millions in annual revenue.Yang arrived at the University of Illinois in 2008 expecting an ordinary first year. Only weeks into the semester, a nosebleed led doctors to discover that his body had an extremely low platelet count, creating a life-threatening situation. At one stage, he was told he had only hours left to live. He recovered, but the journey was far from quick. The following two years were marked by repeated hospital admissions and lengthy treatment, forcing him to put much of his education and personal life on hold while focusing on getting well.Hospital life can be isolating, and Yang found an escape in online games that allowed him to stay mentally engaged despite his circumstances. As reported by Fortune, titles including League of Legends, Minecraft and World of Warcraft became a regular part of his daily routine.Reflecting on that period, he said the experience completely altered the way he thought about games and their role in people's lives. "Games like League of Legends weren’t really made to help me, but in the end, they basically saved my life. What if I start making games with the intention to help people? What kind of power would that be able to unlock?"Rather than seeing games simply as products, he began wondering whether they could leave a lasting emotional impression on players.Reportedly, after moving closer to home, Yang continued his studies at the University of Colorado Boulder, where he enrolled in business. During that time, he put together the early plans for Serenity Forge. The company began with an investment of just $1,000 and a simple guiding statement written while he was still a student: "We create meaningful and emotionally impactful experiences that challenge the way you think. "That idea became the centre of the business instead of serving as marketing language. As reported by Fortune, more than a decade later, Serenity Forge has expanded into a studio of more than 40 employees, publishing around 70 games. Among its best-known releases are Lifeless Planet and Doki Doki Literature Club, the latter reaching more than 30 million downloads. Reportedly, the business now generates annual revenue estimated at between $10 million and $15 million.Before launching his own company, Yang completed internships with Wells Fargo and the Federal Reserve. Yet he often points to an entirely different influence when discussing how Serenity Forge operates.A quote from Whole Foods co-founder and former chief executive John Mackey stayed with him during university: "Just as people cannot live without eating, so a business cannot live without profits. But most people don’t live to eat, and neither must a business live just to make profits."Yang adopted that principle as a way of thinking about long-term decision-making. Revenue remains necessary, but he argues it should support a broader purpose rather than becoming the purpose itself.That approach has occasionally meant rejecting projects expected to earn significant amounts of money. Yang says financial forecasts alone are not enough to persuade the studio to take on a game."There are so many games over the years that were pitched to us where we looked at it was like, ‘Yeah, this is gonna make us, like, $20 million but we’re gonna say no to it, because it’s not a Serenity Forge game,’" Yang said. Those decisions can be difficult for a growing company, particularly in a competitive industry where publishers often chase commercial trends. Serenity Forge instead measures potential projects against the values it established from the beginning.Yang says some of the most memorable moments have come away from the office, during meetings with players at gaming events.Fortune reports, "There will be all these fans, teenagers, that would line up, talk to me. They will cry, they would give me hugs and tell me, ‘you’re the reason that I realized that I was in an abusive relationship and I’m now way healthier and way happier because of the art that you created,’”."That, I think, has always been the thing that drives me way more so than the bottom line or like your employee count or all the other stuff."For him, those conversations have reinforced the direction the company chose many years ago, even when commercial incentives pointed elsewhere.Yang believes early setbacks are an unavoidable part of building a company. Rather than avoiding mistakes altogether, he argues founders should recognise unsuccessful ideas quickly and keep moving. He points to Rovio Entertainment as an example. Before creating Angry Birds, the Finnish developer released more than 50 games without finding a comparable level of success. Serenity Forge has had similar experiences, with some titles performing far better than others.His advice is not centred on chasing a perfect formula but on responding thoughtfully to changing circumstances. "Life can be complicated. When you’re starting a business to do things, be as nuanced as you can about it, and try to try to keep an open mind about the realities of the world."That perspective has shaped both the studio's creative choices and the way Yang continues to approach the business that grew out of an experience he never expected to endure.
Article Summary: Zhenghua Yang's life-threatening illness became the foundation of Serenity Forge. The company began with an investment of just $1,000 and a guiding statement written while he was still a student. More than a decade later, it has expanded into a studio of more than 40 employees, publishing 70 games.
